summary: A guide for small business owners on building an Emergency Response Plan (ERP) with a focus on mobilizing and managing resources, framed by outages and disasters since September 2023. It lays out eight steps, from risk assessment and supplier networks to training, communication, finance, plan review, and community help. Each step is illustrated with quotes and examples from named local business owners and a consultant.
one_line: Eight-step blueprint for small businesses to mobilize and manage resources in emergency response planning, illustrated by real business owner examples from 2023-2024 crises.
key_facts: FEMA defines an Emergency Response Plan (ERP) as "a document that outlines how a business will continue operating during an unplanned event."

Jane Smith, an emergency planning consultant, has guided small businesses through recovery after the blackout on September 12, 2023, and says an ERP is "ineffectual without proper resource management."
Dustin Green, owner of Green's Groceries, coped with the citywide internet outage of November 2023 by having manual card machines and extra cash ready.
Step 1 is risk assessment and resource inventory, covering emergency kits, backup power, communication devices, specialized equipment, and key team members.
During the 'Great Freeze' of late September 2023, many small businesses stayed afloat by pooling resources and sharing inventory.
Sarah Gomez, owner of Tech Solutions, helped form a local business alliance that shared generators and fuel during power disruptions.
On October 17, 2023, Mike Johnson's hardware store kept running during a sudden storm because its emergency supplies were stored in a waterproof container at the back.
Carol Lee's marketing firm stayed unscathed in a December 2023 cybersecurity breach thanks to bi-monthly drills and up-to-date crisis response training.
After the telecom disruption of late October 2023, many small businesses with satellite phones kept in touch with critical stakeholders.
The guide recommends a multi-channel communication strategy that could include radios, smartphones, social media, and bulletin boards.
Jack Martinez, a café owner hit by the November 2023 city power outage, relied on an emergency fund and says a savings buffer can mean the difference between staying open and shutting down.
Elizabeth Brown of Lizzie's Deli revamped her emergency strategy after a fire scare in early January 2024, upgrading fire suppression and training every new hire in basic firefighting.
A local business network initiated by Green and Gomez provided shelter and supplies to residents affected by floods in mid-September 2023.
